title: Spinning Leicester Longwool
subtitle: A foundational British longwool breed with excellent lock structure and strong lustre
excerpt: Leicester Longwool is the parent breed of much of the modern British longwool flock. The locks are long (15 to 25 cm), well-defined, and highly lustrous. Spun worsted it gives an exceptionally smooth, strong yarn; left loosely spun it makes a striking textural yarn for tapestry.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional British longwool spinning practice. The Leicester Longwool breed was developed in the 18th century and is documented in the agricultural literature from Bakewell onward; spinning characteristics draw on standard guild workshop guidance for longwool breeds.

glossaryTerms.definition: A spinning technique where fibres are combed parallel before spinning and drafting happens ahead of the twist, producing a smooth, strong yarn.
The length of an individual lock or aligned group of fibres, measured from the cut end to the tip.
The natural sheen of a longwool fibre, produced by the flat scale structure of the outer cuticle. More light reflects off a flat scale than a corrugated one.

attrs.title: Wool dust
attrs.body: Combing and prepping longwool throws fibre dust. Work in a ventilated space and damp-mop the floor afterwards.

items.name: Spinning wheel with a moderate ratio (6:1 to 8:1)

content.text: Leicester Longwool locks are well-defined and often clean enough to spin directly from the raw fleece after a hand wash. Align each lock by drawing it through a hackle once from the cut end toward the tip. The locks pull out easily because the fibres are smooth and long; unlike fine wools they do not snag or pill during preparation. If you are spinning from commercially-prepared top, draw the top into a continuous pencil-thickness rope before spinning.

Set the wheel to a ratio of 6:1 to 8:1 and use a moderate scotch-tension take-up. The drafting zone is long (15 to 20 cm) because the fibre length demands it. Draft with the worsted method, keeping the twist behind the front hand until a full draft length has been drawn. The Leicester's lock structure drafts cleanly; the main risk is adding too much twist, which makes the yarn stiff. Spin at a pace that keeps the twist moderate.

Ply two singles together at a ratio slightly below the singles twist, so the finished yarn is balanced. Leicester Longwool yarn should feel strong and smooth, not wiry. Skein on the niddy-noddy, soak in warm water, snap to set, and dry hanging under slight tension to preserve the lustre. The yarn blooms very little after washing.

items.problem: The yarn is stiff and wiry
items.cause: Over-twist: the long fibres grip well without much twist, and adding too much makes the yarn inelastic and stiff
items.fix: Reduce treadle speed or increase draft speed so less twist enters each length of fibre. Test by letting a short length of singles twist back on itself: it should coil softly, not spring back hard.

items.problem: The finished yarn has little lustre
items.cause: The fibre was carded rather than combed, scrambling the fibre alignment and reducing the surface reflectivity
items.fix: Prepare by hackling or drawing straight from the lock. Carding is appropriate for woollen-spun breeds; for lustre longwools it destroys the quality that makes them worth spinning.
